Space tops Singaporeans' home wish list, but affordability is the biggest hurdle to buying: ERA survey
article:
Singaporeans want more space in their next home, but affordability remains the top deterrent to buying a property, according to real estate agency ERA Singapore’s My Dream Home Survey 2026.

The online survey, conducted with Ngee Ann Polytechnic between July and August, polled 1,096 people across four generations: Gen Z (aged 14 to 29), Millennials (30 to 45), Gen X (46 to 61) and Baby Boomers (62 and above).

Unsurprisingly, homeownership rises with age, with the proportion of owners making up 24% of Gen Z, 69% of Millennials, 84% of Gen X and 96% of Baby Boomers.

Explore comprehensive data about all ECs , including the average profit at 5 and 10 years

About two-thirds of Singaporeans surveyed plan to buy a residential property, and this includes 28% who intend to do so within three years.

Among those planning to buy within three years, 28% chose condos (15% new launches and 13% resale). Standard Build-To-Order flats were next at 21%, followed by HDB resale flats at 19%.

Among those considering new private condos, 44% have a budget of $1 million to $2 million, while 25% are prepared to spend $2 million to $3 million. Another 8% have a budget of $3 million to $5 million, and 2% are willing to spend more than $5 million.

For resale condos, the split stands at 48% for the $1 million to $2 million budget, followed by 20% for the $2 million to $3 million range. Another 7% plan to spend $3 million to $5 million,  and 2% are prepared to fork out over $5 million.

Space was observed to be a priority. Larger floor plans were favoured by 88% of Millennials, 75% of Gen X and 70% of Gen Z.

Flexible layouts also mattered to Gen Z (61%) and Millennials (60%).

Although seven in 10 Gen Z respondents preferred larger units, 41% said they are currently unable to pursue their dream home. Most are students who are still living with their parents or relatives.

Affordability was the top deterrent to buying a home (30%), followed by additional buyer’s stamp duty (20%) and high property taxes (19%).

Almost four in 10 of Gen Z respondents found it challenging to afford a home now, and 20% said they lack the knowledge and confidence to enter the market.

Marcus Chu, CEO of ERA Singapore, said in a Nov 23 release that buyers are "increasingly weighing their aspirations" against what makes sense for their families, lifestyles and finances.

The location of the home was a key consideration too. Proximity to public transport was a priority for 88% of respondents. Shopping malls (63%), supermarkets (59%) and markets or hawker centres (55%) were also cited as the most sought-after conveniences nearby.

The survey also found that property remained a preferred asset. Some 92% of respondents preferred owning to renting and 87% saw property as a reliable long-term wealth-building vehicle.

Interest in executive condos fell to 10% in the latest survey, from 18% in 2025’s poll, while interest in landed homes rose to 9% from 7%.

Among those considering landed homes, 46% planned to spend more than $3 million, including 23% with a budget above $5 million.

title: KORE US Reit secures full-building tenant at Washington business campus The Westpark Portfolio
article:
The manager of KORE US Reit has secured a tenant for Building C at The Westpark Portfolio, a business campus under its portfolio in located in Redmond, Washington.

In a Nov 23 bourse filing, the Reit’s manager said it has leased the entire building, totaling over 56,000 sq ft, to an aerospace technology company on a seven-year lease. The tenant will use the space for office as well as R&D operations.

The lease lifts committed occupancy at The Westpark Portfolio from 77.7% to 83.7%. It also lift’s KORE US Reit’s overall committed portfolio occupancy from 86.1% to 87.3% on a pro forma basis.

“Securing a full-building lease with a high-quality aerospace technology company underscores the continued demand for well-located office and flex space that can accommodate R&D, manufacturing and testing of products in key innovation markets such as Redmond,” said David Snyder, CEO of KORE US Reit’s manager.

The Westpark Portfolio is a freehold business campus comprising 19 office and flex buildings, along with two industrial buildings. The campus spans 41 acres (16.6ha) and includes a fitness centre, an amenity centre with conference facilities and a tenant lounge.

title: Sheng Siong’s Share Price Has Dropped 34% – Here’s the 1 Metric Investors Should Watch
article:
Shares of
Sheng Siong
(SGX: OV8) have fallen by over 34% since they hit a high of S$3.46 back in July 2026.
So, what happened?
Here’s a clue: for the third quarter of 2026 (3Q2026), the supermarket operator’s revenue grew at its slowest pace of the year.
At first glance, you might think the business is running out of steam.
But take a deeper look, and the slowdown starts to make sense.
What was Sheng Siong up against?
Revenue rose 6.2% year on year (YoY) to S$441.5 million in 3Q2026.
That followed growth of 12.4% in 1Q2026 and 11.3% in 2Q2026.
The year-ago quarter gives you another clue to the gap.
In 3Q’25, revenue grew 14.4%, the fastest of any quarter that year.
Singaporeans began receiving SG60 vouchers from 1 July 2025, which lifted that quarter’s sales.
So in 3Q2026, Sheng Siong had to beat a voucher-boosted quarter.
What is the one metric that gives you a clearer picture?
Compare each quarter with the same quarter two years earlier.
This two-year growth rate looks past the voucher effect in 3Q’25.

On this measure, 3Q2026 revenue was 21.6% higher than in 3Q2024.
That beats the two-year growth of 20.4% for 1Q2026 and 19.1% for 2Q2026.
In other words, 3Q2026 was Sheng Siong’s strongest quarter of the year on a two-year view.
The slowdown says more about last year’s voucher-fuelled sprint than this year’s pace.
The wider market points the same way.
National supermarket and hypermarket sales fell 2.6% YoY in July 2026 and rose just 1.6% in August.
Sheng Siong’s Singapore revenue grew 6.8% for the quarter.
Where is the growth coming from?
For the first nine months of 2026 (9M2026), revenue rose 9.9% to nearly S$1.3 billion.
Most of that growth came from new stores.
The 19 stores opened since the start of 2025 contributed 9.5 percentage points.
Comparable same stores added 1.9 points.
Two store closures took away 1.2 points, and the stores in China another 0.3 points.
Sheng Siong’s retail area in Singapore grew 10.5% YoY to 799,800 square feet.
The grocer is also opening stores faster than planned.
It opened seven new stores in 9M2026, more than double management’s aim of
at least three a year
.
Four public tenders are awaiting results.
Is the growth reaching the bottom line?
Gross margin climbed to 32.2% in 3Q2026 from 31.5% a year ago.
For context, gross margin stood at 29.4% in 2022 and has risen every year since.
Higher costs ate into those gains.
Staff costs rose 14.4% for 9M2026.
A larger store count and higher bonuses pushed the wage bill up. So did the pay rises under the Progressive Wage Model in September 2025.
Operating profit grew 3.4% in 3Q2026, while net profit rose just 1.9% to S$44.6 million.
Why did free cash flow fall?
Free cash flow fell 37.6% to S$101.3 million in 9M2026.
That number matters, because free cash flow is the lifeblood of
dividends
.
Here, timing is the culprit.
Sheng Siong paid its vendors earlier, which cut trade payables by S$56.4 million.
Before working capital changes, operating cash flow rose 13.1% to S$203.6 million.
The supermarket operator ended September with S$388.9 million in cash and no borrowings.
For income investors, the dividend
growth story
looks intact.
Get Smart: What to watch next
The main risk is the Johor Bahru–Singapore RTS Link, expected to open in February 2027.
Management says the link may increase cross-border shopping for selected packaged groceries and household products.
A February start means 1Q2027 will give an initial read on the impact.
Comparable same-store sales in 2Q2027 will be the first full-quarter test.
